gloss_terse: Harum, a Judahite name appearing in 1 Chronicles 4:8, possibly related to Sabaean and Arabic personal names
gloss_readable: Harum appears as a personal name in the genealogy of Judah, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 4:8. The name finds parallels in Sabaean inscriptions (הרם, הרמה) and Arabic onomastics (هِرْمٌ), suggesting it may belong to a broader Semitic naming pattern. The name's single occurrence makes its precise meaning uncertain, though comparative evidence points to authenticity.

senses.1: This personal name occurs uniquely in the tribal genealogies of Judah. Spanish and English transliterations preserve the Hebrew consonantal framework (Harum), while French and German sources bracket the form, indicating textual uncertainty. The comparative Semitic evidence from Sabaean and Arabic sources strengthens the case for this as a genuine ancient name rather than textual corruption.

gloss_terse: Harmon, a disputed place name in Amos 4:3, possibly Armenia or another location; the text may be corrupt
gloss_readable: This word appears in a difficult passage in Amos 4:3, where judgment is pronounced on Samaria's elite. Ancient versions disagree wildly: Targum and Peshitta read 'mountains of Armenia,' while the Hebrew may be corrupt. If sound, it designates some destination of exile, though the specific location is lost to us. The similarity to 'palace' (ארמון) tempted early translators but seems linguistically improbable.

senses.1: French renders this as 'palais' (palace), following the similarity to ארמון, while Spanish offers 'hacia-Harmón' (toward Harmon) preserving a place name reading. The ancient versions' interpretation as Armenia (mountains thereof) suggests a distant land of exile. The single occurrence and textual uncertainty make confident identification impossible, though the context clearly involves forcible removal from the land.

gloss_terse: Destruction, specifically in the wordplay 'city of destruction' (Isaiah 19:18) contrasting with 'city of the sun'
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears in Isaiah's oracle concerning Egypt, in the phrase 'city of destruction' (עִיר הַהֶרֶס). Most interpreters see deliberate wordplay: what was once called 'city of the sun' (Heliopolis, עִיר הַחֶרֶס) will be renamed 'city of destruction' after its temples fall. Some ancient manuscripts read 'city of righteousness' instead, suggesting early textual variation or intentional alteration. The multilingual glosses consistently emphasize destruction, aligned with the Hebrew's aggressive prophetic tone.

senses.1: Multilingual evidence uniformly captures the semantic force of destruction: Spanish 'la-destrucción,' English 'the-destruction.' The term appears in a context of divine judgment against Egyptian idolatry, with the definite article emphasizing a specific, fated overthrow. The single occurrence in Isaiah 19:18 makes this a highly contextualized term, its meaning bound to the specific prophetic announcement of temple destruction in Heliopolis.

gloss_terse: Hashem, a personal name in 1 Chronicles 11:34; textual issues suggest reading 'Jashen' from 2 Samuel 23:32
gloss_readable: Hashem appears as the father of one of David's warriors in 1 Chronicles 11:34, but the parallel text in 2 Samuel 23:32 reads 'Jashen' instead, with 'sons of' deleted. Most scholars regard this as textual corruption rather than a distinct person. The name itself is intriguing—literally 'the Name,' a common reverential substitution for the divine name in later Jewish tradition—but that usage postdates this text considerably.

senses.1: All major translations simply transliterate the form: Spanish 'Hasém,' English 'HaShem,' while French and German bracket it signaling textual doubt. The textual parallel with יָשֵׁן (Jashen) in 2 Samuel strongly suggests scribal error. Despite the name's later significance as a reverent circumlocution for God's name, here it functions as a personal name in a genealogical list, albeit one that likely originated through textual corruption.

gloss_terse: A causing to hear, bringing tidings in person (Ezekiel 24:26); possibly an Aramaizing infinitive construct
gloss_readable: This unique form appears in Ezekiel's oracle about Jerusalem's fall, describing someone who will 'cause ears to hear'—that is, bring news in person. The construction is unusual, possibly an Aramaizing Hiphil infinitive. Some scholars propose emending to a simpler reading, but the Hebrew as it stands conveys the idea of direct oral report, the messenger arriving to announce the city's destruction. French renders 'communication' capturing the communicative act rather than literal hearing.

senses.1: The multilingual glosses reveal interpretive range: Spanish 'para-hacer-oír' (to cause to hear) preserves the causative force, while English 'to-cause-to-hear' does likewise. French 'communication' abstracts to the functional purpose. The context in Ezekiel 24:26 specifies that a refugee will arrive to deliver the news of Jerusalem's fall directly, emphasizing personal, oral communication in an era before mass media—news traveled by foot and voice.

gloss_terse: Melting, specifically 'like melting of silver' in a smelting furnace (Ezekiel 22:22)
gloss_readable: This noun describes the process of silver melting in a crucible, appearing in Ezekiel's extended metallurgical metaphor for divine judgment. The form itself is morphologically interesting—a Hophal-pattern noun with dissimilation from an expected הֻתּוּךְ. Ezekiel uses smelting imagery throughout chapter 22 to depict God's purifying judgment on Jerusalem: as silver melts in the furnace, so the city will melt under divine wrath.

senses.1: Spanish 'Como-se-funde' (as it melts) and English 'as-melting-of' both capture the comparative simile structure of Ezekiel 22:22. French 'fondre' (to melt) emphasizes the action itself. The single occurrence makes this a highly specialized term, bound to Ezekiel's prophetic rhetoric. The imagery is vivid: intense heat, liquefaction, the breakdown of solid structures—all metaphors for God's consuming judgment on a corrupt city.

gloss_terse: To mock, deceive (Piel); Elijah mocking the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18:27
gloss_readable: This verb appears in one of Scripture's most dramatic confrontations: Elijah on Mount Carmel, taunting the prophets of Baal as their deity fails to respond. The verb, a secondary formation from the root תלל, carries sharp irony. Elijah's mocking suggestions—perhaps Baal is meditating, or busy, or on a journey, or asleep—drip with sarcasm. The multilingual glosses universally capture the derisive tone.

senses.1: Spanish 'y-se-burló' (and he mocked), English 'and-mocked,' French 'et-mocked'—all preserve the narrative past tense and the confrontational edge. The single occurrence in 1 Kings 18:27 is iconic in biblical literature: prophetic satire directed at pagan worship. Elijah's mockery exposes the impotence of Baal and the folly of those who serve him, setting up the dramatic theophany that follows when YHWH answers by fire.

gloss_terse: Mockery, mocking (plural noun); Job's complaint that mockery surrounds him (Job 17:2)
gloss_readable: Job uses this plural noun to describe his situation: mockery on every side. In a passage lamenting his social alienation and physical suffering, he declares that mockers surround him, his eye dwelling on their provocations. The noun derives from the same root as the verb in 1 Kings 18:27 (Elijah mocking Baal's prophets), but here the semantic focus shifts from the act to the agents—the mockers themselves.

senses.1: English and Spanish render as 'mockers,' 'burladores'—focusing on the people who mock rather than the abstract concept. This interpretive move reflects the plural form and Job's context: he's surrounded by hostile individuals, not merely an atmosphere of derision. The single occurrence in Job 17:2 contributes to the book's portrait of Job's social suffering—physical pain compounded by communal rejection and ridicule from those who should offer comfort.

gloss_terse: To shout at, attack (possibly); text uncertain in Psalm 62:3, where mockers conspire against a righteous person
gloss_readable: The meaning and even the root of this verb remain disputed. In Psalm 62:3, it describes hostile action against an individual—either shouting at, threatening, or attacking. Some scholars derive it from a root meaning 'shout at' (Arabic cognates suggest threatening cries), while others propose emendation to 'be frantic against.' The multilingual glosses diverge, reflecting the textual uncertainty. The context is clear enough: enemies conspiring to topple someone of standing.

senses.1: Spanish 'atacaréis' (you will attack) and English 'will-you-attack' interpret as physical assault, while French 'conspirer' (to conspire) emphasizes coordinated hostility. German follows the attack interpretation. The single occurrence and textual difficulties prevent certainty, but the psalm's context—a meditation on trust in God amid human threats—supports a meaning of aggressive, coordinated hostility aimed at bringing down the righteous.

gloss_terse: Vedan (or Wedan), a disputed place name in Ezekiel 27:19; possibly textual corruption or unknown trading partner
gloss_readable: This word appears in Ezekiel's oracle against Tyre, listing trading partners. The identification is wholly uncertain. Some manuscripts omit it entirely; others read it alongside 'Javan' (Greece/Ionia), creating 'Vedan and Javan.' Proposed solutions include Waddān near Medina, the Arabian Arnabani mentioned in Assyrian records, or simply textual corruption. The mention of wine in the context might help identify the location, but certainty eludes us.

senses.1: Translations reflect confusion: Spanish 'Y-Dan' (and Dan), English 'and-Dan,' French 'et-Vedan,' German 'und-Dan.' Some read this as the Israelite tribal territory Dan (unlikely in this context), others as an otherwise unknown locale. The single occurrence in Ezekiel 27:19, embedded in a damaged text listing exotic trade goods, leaves the identification suspended between plausible conjectures and frank acknowledgment of ignorance.

gloss_terse: Waheb, an unknown place name in Numbers 21:14, part of a fragmentary quotation from the 'Book of YHWH's Wars'
gloss_readable: This appears in one of Scripture's most tantalizing fragments: a quotation from the otherwise lost 'Book of the Wars of YHWH.' The text is broken—apparently a verb has dropped out—and Waheb's location is unknown. Ancient versions transliterate without explanation. Modern attempts to identify it with Sahidic topography or to emend the text to 'gold' (זָהָב) remain speculative. We possess a name severed from its context, a fossil from ancient Israelite poetry.

senses.1: All four languages simply transliterate: Spanish 'Vaheb,' English 'Waheb,' French 'Waheb,' German 'Waheb.' The unanimous choice to preserve the Hebrew form reflects scholarly humility: we don't know what or where Waheb was. Numbers 21:14 preserves ancient battle poetry celebrating YHWH's victories in the wilderness, but the fragmentary preservation means the geographical reference remains opaque to modern readers.

gloss_terse: Guilty, criminal (adjective); describing a crooked path in Proverbs 21:8, though the text may be corrupt
gloss_readable: This adjective appears in Proverbs 21:8's contrast between the guilty and the pure: 'Crooked is the way of a guilty man.' However, textual critics suspect dittography—accidental repetition creating וָזָר from an original pair וְזַךְ ('and pure'). If the text is sound, the word denotes moral guilt or criminality, contrasting with uprightness. Spanish and English preserve 'guilty,' 'culpable,' while French and German bracket the term, signaling doubt.

senses.1: The moral-legal domain is clear in Spanish 'culpable' and English 'guilty'—someone bearing blame, following crooked paths. Proverbs uses spatial imagery (crooked vs. straight) to depict moral character, and this adjective, if original, would contribute to that pattern. The single occurrence and textual uncertainty make confident interpretation difficult, though the semantic field of guilt and moral crookedness fits Proverbs' didactic rhetoric well.

gloss_terse: Vaizatha, a Persian name—one of Haman's ten sons executed in Esther 9:9, possibly meaning 'given-of-the-Best-One'
gloss_readable: Vaizatha appears in the grim list of Haman's ten sons, all hanged on the same day in the book of Esther. Scholars identify the name as Persian, possibly Vahyazdāta, meaning something like 'given by the Best One' (a Zoroastrian divine title). The name's appearance in this literary context—the reversal of fortunes, the poetic justice of Haman's line being destroyed—gives it narrative weight beyond mere onomastic interest.

senses.1: Spanish 'Vayzata' and English 'Vaizatha' attempt phonetic approximation of the Persian original, while French and German bracket the form, acknowledging the foreign name's complexity. All ten sons receive Persian names, grounding Esther's narrative in the Achaemenid imperial context. The execution of Vaizatha and his brothers in Esther 9:9 completes the reversal motif central to the book: the gallows prepared for Mordecai becomes the instrument of Haman's family's destruction.

gloss_terse: Child, offspring; Sarah described as having 'no child' (Genesis 11:30), a rare synonym for the common yeled
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears in the description of Sarah's barrenness before Isaac's miraculous birth: 'she had no child' (Genesis 11:30). The term is a synonym of the far more common yeled, apparently cognate to Arabic walad and Ethiopic wald. Its rarity in Biblical Hebrew may reflect dialectal or stylistic variation. The context—childlessness as crisis, prelude to divine intervention—charges this simple noun with narrative tension.

senses.1: Spanish 'hijo' (son/child), English 'a-child,' French 'un-enfant,' German 'ein-Kind'—all use the most common word for offspring in their respective languages, reflecting this term's basic semantic value. Genesis 11:30's statement 'Sarai had no child' sets up the Abraham-Sarah cycle's central drama: the promise of countless descendants to a barren couple. This rare vocabulary choice marks the passage's significance, the absence that will drive the narrative forward.

gloss_terse: Vanyah, a personal name in Ezra 10:36; one of those who married foreign women, though text is uncertain
gloss_readable: Vanyah appears in Ezra's list of men who had married foreign women during the exile and were compelled to divorce them. The name occurs only here, and ancient versions disagree on the spelling, suggesting textual corruption. Greek manuscripts offer wildly variant forms, indicating the scribes themselves were uncertain. The name's single occurrence in a contested text makes confident analysis impossible, though it functions clearly as a personal name in this genealogical-legal context.

senses.1: Spanish 'Vanyah' and English 'Vanyah' transliterate directly, while French and German bracket the form, signaling textual doubt. Ezra 10 records a painful chapter in post-exilic history: the dissolution of mixed marriages to preserve communal boundaries. Vanyah's inclusion in this list marks him as someone who navigated the complex social and religious tensions of the return from Babylon, though we know nothing else about him.

gloss_terse: Vophsi, father of Nahbi from the tribe of Naphtali (Numbers 13:14); a spy sent to scout Canaan
gloss_readable: Vophsi is mentioned as the father of Nahbi, one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan. The name appears only here, and even the ancient Greek versions show textual variation, rendering the patronymic differently. As with many names in the spy narrative, this one anchors a representative in a specific family and tribe—in this case, Naphtali—lending historical specificity to the wilderness generation's pivotal moment of faithlessness.

senses.1: All four translations simply transliterate: 'Vophsi' in Spanish, English, and French, with German matching. Numbers 13 establishes the framework for one of Israel's great failures: the refusal to enter the land after hearing the majority report from the spies. Vophsi's son Nahbi participated in that reconnaissance mission, though the text doesn't specify whether he stood with the faithful minority (Joshua and Caleb) or the fearful majority.

gloss_terse: Vashni, apparently a corrupted reading in 1 Chronicles 6:28; should be 'and the second' based on 1 Samuel 8:2
gloss_readable: The Masoretic Text of 1 Chronicles 6:28 appears to give 'Vashni' as the name of Samuel's firstborn son. However, the parallel text in 1 Samuel 8:2 clearly identifies the firstborn as Joel and the second as Abijah. Most scholars conclude that 'Vashni' is a textual error for 'and the second' (וְהַשֵּׁנִי), with Joel's name having dropped out. Ancient versions support this reading, and modern translations often emend accordingly.

senses.1: Spanish renders as 'Vasni' treating it as a name, while English offers 'and-the-second,' German 'und-zweiter'—revealing the interpretive divide. The LXX supports emendation, suggesting early awareness of the problem. This appears to be a case where scribal error created a 'ghost name' that never actually existed. First Chronicles' tendency to preserve damaged genealogical material means such textual difficulties are not uncommon in its lists.

gloss_terse: To endow, bestow (verb); Leah's wordplay on Zebulun's name, 'God has endowed me' (Genesis 30:20)
gloss_readable: This verb appears in Leah's etymological explanation of her son Zebulun's name. She declares, 'God has endowed me with a good endowment'—a wordplay connecting the son's name to the concept of bestowing gifts or dowry. The root has Aramaic cognates meaning 'dowry' and appears in various Semitic languages. Genesis 30:20 offers two explanations for Zebulun's name (the other involving 'dwelling'), reflecting the biblical fondness for multiple folk etymologies.

senses.1: Spanish 'dotó-me' (endowed me), English 'endowed-me,' French 'endowed-moi'—all preserve the perfect tense and the sense of divine gift-giving. Leah's declaration comes after bearing six sons and marks a shift in her self-understanding: no longer merely competing with Rachel, she now sees herself as divinely enriched. The verb's semantic range includes dowry, bestowal, and endowment, all suggesting valuable gifts that elevate the recipient's status.

gloss_terse: Endowment, gift (noun); Leah's 'good endowment' from God in the naming of Zebulun (Genesis 30:20)
gloss_readable: This noun complements the verb in Genesis 30:20, forming Leah's declaration: 'God has endowed me with a good endowment.' The doubling of the root (verbal and nominal forms) creates emphasis and wordplay typical of biblical naming narratives. The term specifically denotes a gift or dowry, something of value bestowed to enhance status or establish relationship. Leah's sixth son represents not just another child but a mark of divine favor.

senses.1: Spanish 'dote' (dowry), English 'endowment,' German 'ein-Geschenk' (a gift)—all emphasize the value-transfer aspect. French matches English. The use of dowry language is telling: Leah frames her fertility as God's enrichment of her, compensating perhaps for Jacob's preferential love for Rachel. The 'good endowment' transforms biological reproduction into theological affirmation, Leah reading her maternal success as divine vindication.

gloss_terse: Zabud, an officer of Solomon (1 Kings 4:5); the name means 'bestowed' or 'endowed'
gloss_readable: Zabud appears in the administrative list of Solomon's officials as a priest and 'the king's friend,' a title suggesting special advisory status. The name derives from the root meaning 'bestow' or 'endow,' suggesting perhaps that he was seen as a gift. First Kings 4 catalogs Solomon's bureaucratic apparatus at the height of his power, and Zabud's dual role as priest and royal confidant reflects the integration of religious and political authority in the united monarchy.

senses.1: All translations simply add 'and' to the transliteration: Spanish 'y-Zabud,' English 'and-Zabud,' French 'et-Zabud,' German 'und-Zabud.' The coordination reflects the list structure of 1 Kings 4. Zabud's designation as 'the king's friend' is significant—a technical term for a trusted advisor, appearing elsewhere in ancient Near Eastern courts. His presence in this list marks him as part of Solomon's inner circle during Israel's golden age.

gloss_terse: Zabud (variant spelling in Ezra 8:14 Ketiv); the Qere reads 'Zaccur' instead, indicating textual uncertainty
gloss_readable: The written text (Ketiv) of Ezra 8:14 gives 'Zabud' as the name of a returned exile, but the marginal reading (Qere) corrects to 'Zaccur.' Ancient versions also vary, with some Greek manuscripts supporting one reading, others the other. This reflects the textual fluidity of genealogical lists, where similar-sounding names could be confused in transmission. The context is the list of families returning from Babylonian exile, where accurate preservation of names mattered for property claims and tribal identity.

senses.1: Translations bracket the form, acknowledging uncertainty: Spanish '[y-Zabud],' English '[and-Zavud],' French '[וזבוד],' German '[[וזבוד]].' The double-bracketing in German signals even deeper doubt. Ezra's lists of returnees were crucial documents for the restoration community, establishing who had legitimate claim to ancestral property and temple service. Textual variants in such lists suggest the difficulties of maintaining accurate records through the trauma of exile and return.

gloss_terse: Zebina, an Aramaic name meaning 'bought' or 'purchased'; one who married a foreign woman (Ezra 10:43)
gloss_readable: Zebina appears in Ezra's list of those who had married foreign women and were compelled to divorce them. The name is Aramaic, from the root meaning 'buy' or 'purchase,' possibly suggesting that the bearer was purchased as a slave or adopted. This reflects the linguistic environment of the post-exilic period, when Aramaic increasingly influenced Hebrew onomastics. The name's occurrence in this painful social-religious crisis list gives it historical specificity but no further narrative development.

senses.1: Spanish 'Zevina' and English 'Zevina' attempt phonetic rendering, while French and German bracket the form. The Aramaic etymology ('bought') is intriguing—was Zebina a slave who gained freedom, a purchased child, or is the name purely conventional? Ezra 10 records a community attempting to maintain religious and ethnic boundaries in the vulnerable early post-exilic period, and Zebina's inclusion shows he was caught in that painful process of communal redefinition.

gloss_terse: To honor, exalt (verb); Leah's alternate wordplay on Zebulun, 'my husband will honor me' (Genesis 30:20)
gloss_readable: This verb provides the second etymology for Zebulun's name in Genesis 30:20: 'Now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.' The root appears in Akkadian (zabālu, 'exalt') and possibly Phoenician onomastics. Leah's two explanations for Zebulun—divine endowment and marital honor—reflect her dual desires: divine recognition and her husband's affection. The wordplay enriches the narrative, showing Leah's complex emotional world.

senses.1: Spanish 'morará-conmigo' (will dwell with me) follows an alternative interpretation deriving the verb from a root meaning 'dwell,' while English 'will-honor-me' and French follow the 'honor' interpretation. German offers 'wird-bei-mir-wohnen' (will dwell with me), siding with the dwelling interpretation. The divide reflects ancient uncertainty about the root. Leah's hope—whether for honor or dwelling-together—expresses her longing for Jacob's presence and esteem after bearing six sons.

gloss_terse: To buy, gain (Aramaic verb); 'you are trying to gain time' in Daniel 2:8
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb appears in King Nebuchadnezzar's accusation against his counselors: 'I know that you are trying to gain time.' The root means 'buy' or 'purchase' in various Aramaic dialects and appears in Nabataean and Palmyrene inscriptions. Here it's used metaphorically: buying or purchasing time, stalling. The idiom captures Nebuchadnezzar's impatience with his advisors' excuses, his suspicion that they're dodging the impossible task he's set them.

senses.1: Spanish 'estáis-comprando' (you are buying), English 'are-buying,' French 'essayer' (to try)—the translations reflect the metaphor. French abstracts from the commercial imagery to the purpose (trying/attempting), while Spanish and English preserve the literal 'buying.' Daniel 2:8 captures a moment of royal frustration: the king knows his demand is unreasonable (tell me both the dream and its interpretation without my describing the dream!), and he suspects his advisors are stalling for time, hoping the crisis will pass.

gloss_terse: Grape skin; part of what a Nazirite must avoid eating (Numbers 6:4), possibly the transparent outer skin
gloss_readable: This obscure term appears in the Nazirite regulations, specifying that one under the vow must avoid eating anything from the grape vine, 'from the seeds to the skin.' The exact identification is uncertain—possibly the transparent outer skin of the grape. The Mishnah preserves the term with the same meaning. Rabbinic sources connect it to words for 'glass' (זְגוּגִית), suggesting transparency as the linking concept. The term's rarity makes precise definition difficult, but the context clearly involves grape products forbidden to Nazirites.

senses.1: Spanish 'hollejo' (skin/husk), English 'skin,' French 'peau' (skin), German 'Haut' (skin)—unanimous agreement on the basic meaning. Numbers 6:4 establishes comprehensive prohibition: the Nazirite avoids not just wine but every part of the grape, from internal seeds to external skin. This totality reflects the vow's radical separation, the Nazirite's complete abstention from the fruit that symbolizes settled agricultural life and its pleasures.

gloss_terse: To make loathsome (Piel); Job's life makes food loathsome to him due to suffering (Job 33:20)
gloss_readable: This Piel verb describes how suffering affects Job's appetite: 'his life makes bread loathsome to him.' The root means 'be foul' or 'fetid' in various Semitic languages; here the causative stem indicates that Job's suffering causes him to loathe even desirable food. The parallel clause mentions his soul loathing 'food of desire,' reinforcing the image of sickness so severe it destroys appetite. The verb captures physical and psychological revulsion, suffering that penetrates to basic bodily needs.

senses.1: Spanish 'Y-aborrece' (and loathes), English 'and-loathes-him'—both capture the strong aversion. The grammatical form is unusual enough that some scholars suspect textual corruption, but the sense is clear: extreme suffering destroys even the desire for food. Job 33:20 appears in Elihu's speech, describing how God uses suffering to discipline and save. The vivid image of food becoming repulsive conveys suffering's totalizing effect, how it transforms even life's basic pleasures into sources of disgust.

gloss_terse: Zaham, son of King Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:19); name possibly related to the root meaning 'foul' or 'loathsome'
gloss_readable: Zaham appears in the genealogy of Rehoboam, one of his sons by Mahalath. The name's derivation from the root meaning 'foul' or 'loathsome' (if that's indeed the etymology) is puzzling—why would parents choose such a name? Perhaps it had a different connotation in that period, or perhaps it's an apotropaic name meant to ward off evil. Second Chronicles preserves it without comment, simply listing Zaham among Rehoboam's numerous offspring.

senses.1: All translations simply transliterate: Spanish 'Zaham,' English 'Zaham,' with French and German bracketing. The single occurrence provides no narrative context beyond the bare genealogical notice. Rehoboam's family life, detailed in 2 Chronicles 11, includes multiple wives and concubines and many children, reflecting royal polygamy's dynastic ambitions. Zaham is one name among many, his life unrecorded beyond this genealogical anchor point.

gloss_terse: To shine, give light (Hiphil); the wise 'shall shine' in everlasting glory (Daniel 12:3)
gloss_readable: This Hiphil verb appears in Daniel's vision of the resurrection and final judgment: 'those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament.' The imagery of light represents eschatological glory, the vindication and exaltation of the righteous teachers who endured persecution. The verb derives from a root meaning 'shine' or 'be bright,' cognate with Arabic and Aramaic forms. Daniel uses astronomical imagery—firmament, stars—to convey the transcendent, everlasting nature of this glory.

senses.1: Spanish 'brillarán' (they will shine), English 'shall-shine'—both preserve the future glory aspect. French offers 'avertir' (to warn), apparently deriving from a different root (the homonym meaning 'warn'). Daniel 12:3 is a pivotal text for resurrection hope and eschatological reward. The shining of the wise contrasts with the darkness of judgment, their light everlasting like the stars, a beacon of divine vindication for those who suffered for righteousness.

gloss_terse: To be warned, careful (Aramaic Peal passive participle); 'be warned' against negligence (Ezra 4:22)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic passive participle appears in a letter from Persian officials warning against allowing Jerusalem's walls to be rebuilt: 'Be warned not to be negligent in this matter.' The root is the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew root meaning 'warn' or 'admonish.' The officials fear that Jerusalem's restoration will lead to rebellion and loss of tax revenue, so they urge the king to vigilance. The verb captures administrative alertness, the bureaucratic imperative to prevent potential threats.

senses.1: Spanish 'Y-cuidadosos' (and careful), English 'and-careful'—both emphasizing the state of alertness rather than the act of warning. Ezra 4:22 records the opposition Judah faced during the rebuilding efforts after the exile. Persian officials, anxious about imperial security and revenue, urged the king to stop the construction. This verb, calling for careful vigilance, reflects the political tensions surrounding the restoration: suspicion, bureaucratic caution, and the vulnerable position of the returned exiles.

gloss_terse: This (feminine demonstrative pronoun); appearing in Hosea 7:16 and Psalm 132:12, an archaic form of zot
gloss_readable: This pronoun is an archaic or variant spelling of the common demonstrative 'this' (feminine). It appears in Hosea 7:16—'this is their derision'—referring to Israel's coming fall by the sword. The form also occurs in Psalm 132:12 as a relative pronoun, 'my testimony which...' The rarity of this spelling compared to the standard form suggests either dialectal variation or archaic usage preserved in poetic contexts.

senses.1: All four translations render as 'this' with variations: Spanish 'esto,' English 'this,' French 'ceci.' The grammatical function is straightforward—pointing to something previously mentioned or contextually present. In Hosea 7:16, 'this' refers to the judgment announced: falling by the sword, becoming an object of derision. The demonstrative makes the divine verdict concrete and immediate, transforming prophetic announcement into inescapable reality.

gloss_terse: To act presumptuously, arrogantly (Aramaic Haphel infinitive); Nebuchadnezzar's prideful behavior (Daniel 5:20)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic infinitive describes Nebuchadnezzar's fatal flaw: his heart became proud and his spirit hardened 'to act presumptuously.' The causative Haphel stem emphasizes deliberate arrogant action. Daniel uses this to explain why Nebuchadnezzar was deposed—his presumption crossed a line, prompting divine judgment. The verb parallels the Hebrew root for arrogance and presumption, and the context (royal hubris, divine humbling) is classic biblical theodicy.

senses.1: Spanish 'con-soberbia' (with pride), English 'to-act-proudly'—both capturing the arrogant disposition. Daniel 5:20 explains that Nebuchadnezzar's presumptuous pride led to his temporary madness and deposition, a cautionary tale Daniel tells Belshazzar to warn against similar hubris. The infinitive emphasizes ongoing, habitual arrogance: not a single act but a pattern of behavior that provoked divine intervention. The story illustrates the danger of royal self-exaltation, the king who forgets his accountability to the King of Heaven.

gloss_terse: The Zuzim, an ancient Transjordanian people defeated in Genesis 14:5; possibly identical with the Zamzummim
gloss_readable: The Zuzim appear in Genesis 14:5 as one of several ancient peoples defeated by the eastern kings in their campaign through Transjordan. They dwelt in a place called Ham, somewhere between Bashan and Moab. Many scholars identify them with the Zamzummim mentioned in Deuteronomy 2:20, suggesting textual variation in the tribal name. Otherwise unknown, they represent the pre-Israelite population that the narrator presents as powerful ('mighty nations' in the Septuagint) but nonetheless defeatable.

senses.1: Spanish 'zuzitas' and English 'the-Zuzim' transliterate the gentilicial form, while French and German add the definite article. Genesis 14 preserves archaic geographical and ethnic information, listing peoples otherwise unknown to us. The Zuzim's defeat by Chedorlaomer and his allies sets the stage for Lot's capture and Abraham's rescue mission. These ancient peoples function narratively as the backdrop against which Abraham's faithfulness and military prowess stand out.

gloss_terse: Zoheth, a descendant of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:20); etymology and meaning unknown
gloss_readable: Zoheth appears in the genealogies of Judah, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 4:20 (also referenced as 'son of Zoheth'). The etymology is uncertain—lexicons offer no clear derivation. Ancient Greek manuscripts vary in their transliterations, suggesting the name was unfamiliar even to early translators. The single occurrence in a genealogical list leaves us with a name anchored to the tribe of Judah but otherwise undefined.

senses.1: Translations universally transliterate: Spanish 'Zojet,' English 'Zocheth,' with French and German bracketing. First Chronicles preserves extensive genealogical material for Judah, and Zoheth is one among many names whose historical persons are lost to us. His inclusion establishes tribal connection and ancestral legitimacy but provides no narrative development. The name survives as a bare record, testimony to a life we know nothing about beyond its place in Judah's lineage.

gloss_terse: Well-fed (Hophal participle); describing lustful horses in Jeremiah 5:8, possibly with sexual connotations
gloss_readable: This Hophal participle describes horses in Jeremiah's indictment of Judah's adultery: 'They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing after his neighbor's wife.' The passive form ('being fed' or 'having been fed') emphasizes their condition—pampered, overfed, driven by appetite rather than need. Some Assyriological studies suggest connections to sexual desire in the cognate root. The image is vivid and unflattering: Israel's wealthy elite, sated and lecherous, pursuing illicit relationships.

senses.1: Spanish 'bien-alimentados' (well-fed) and English 'well-fed' both focus on the alimentary aspect, while the context makes clear this feeding produces sexual excess. Jeremiah 5:8 uses animal imagery to depict moral degradation: like overfed stallions who neigh for mares, Judah's men pursue their neighbors' wives. The metaphor links physical satiety with moral corruption, suggesting that prosperity without righteousness produces lust and social chaos.

gloss_terse: To be fed (Aramaic Hithpael); describing how Nebuchadnezzar was fed from the field during his madness (Daniel 4:12)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic Hithpael verb describes Nebuchadnezzar's condition during his divinely imposed madness: he 'was fed from the grass of the field' like an animal. The reflexive/passive Hithpael indicates he received feeding from the field, emphasizing his degradation from royal luxury to bestial existence. Daniel's vision depicts the king driven from human society, eating grass, until seven times pass and he acknowledges God's sovereignty. The verb captures the humiliation of a ruler reduced to animal status.

senses.1: Spanish 'se-alimentaba' (he fed himself / was fed), English 'was-fed,' French 'nourrir' (to feed)—all convey the passive reception of nourishment from the field. Daniel 4:12's context is judgment and restoration: the proud king who exalted himself must learn dependence through radical humiliation. Being 'fed from the field' like cattle strips Nebuchadnezzar of human dignity, throne, and reason—until the appointed time when he looks up, recognizes Heaven's rule, and is restored.

gloss_terse: To be loathsome, offensive (Qal); Job's breath is loathsome to his wife (Job 19:17)
gloss_readable: This verb describes Job's condition: 'My breath is loathsome to my wife.' Some derive it from the root meaning 'become strange,' implying estrangement and disgust. Others propose a separate root meaning 'be foul' or 'loathsome,' citing Arabic cognates. Either way, the semantic result is similar: suffering has made Job physically repulsive, alienating him even from his spouse. The parallel clause mentions pleading with his wife and brothers, emphasizing his social isolation.

senses.1: Spanish 'es-extraño' (is strange), English 'is-offensive,' French 'étrangère' (strange/foreign)—revealing the interpretive divide between 'strange' and 'loathsome.' Job 19:17's context is profound social suffering: disease has made Job disgusting to those closest to him. Whether the repulsion stems from strangeness or loathsomeness, the effect is the same—isolation, rejection, the breakdown of intimate relationships under the pressure of inexplicable suffering.

gloss_terse: The one crushed, pressed (participle); crushed viper eggs in Isaiah 59:5, metaphor for violence producing violence
gloss_readable: This passive participle appears in Isaiah's indictment: they hatch viper eggs, and 'the one crushed' (the egg that's broken) releases a viper. The verb means 'press' or 'squeeze,' and here it's used in a grim metaphor for violence begetting violence: crushing the egg doesn't destroy the threat, it releases it prematurely. Isaiah 59 catalogs Judah's sins—violence, falsehood, injustice—using vivid imagery of webs and eggs to depict the self-destructive nature of evil.

senses.1: Spanish 'y-lo-que-se-rompe' (and that which breaks), English 'and-the-one-crushed'—both capturing the passive action. The metaphor is striking: even attempting to destroy the eggs (evil plans/acts) results in danger, as the premature viper emerges to strike. Isaiah uses this image to show that Judah's society is saturated with violence—every action, even defensive ones, produces more harm. The crushing becomes a metaphor for futile attempts to escape the consequences of systemic evil.

gloss_terse: Zaza, a descendant of Jerahmeel from the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:33); possibly related to Assyrian name Zazâ
gloss_readable: Zaza appears in the genealogy of Jerahmeel within the tribe of Judah, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 2:33. Scholars note a possible connection to an Assyrian personal name Zazâ, suggesting the name had wider Semitic usage. The etymology remains unclear, and the single biblical occurrence offers no narrative context. Like many names in Chronicles' genealogies, Zaza marks a person's place in Israel's ancestral structure without telling us anything about their life.

senses.1: All translations simply transliterate with coordinating conjunction: Spanish 'y-Zaza,' English 'and-Zaza,' with French and German bracketing. First Chronicles preserves extensive genealogical material for the tribe of Judah, and Zaza is one link in the long chain descending from Jerahmeel. His inclusion establishes tribal connection and territorial claims in the restoration period, though we know nothing of his personal history or significance beyond this genealogical anchor.

gloss_terse: To fear, be afraid (Qal); Elihu held back from speaking out of fear for his elders (Job 32:6)
gloss_readable: This verb, related to Aramaic 'fear,' describes Elihu's initial reticence in the Job dialogue: 'I was afraid and dared not show you my opinion.' The young man defers to his elders, holding back his critique out of reverence and fear. Some interpreters derive the verb from a root meaning 'shrink back,' emphasizing the physical withdrawal that accompanies fear. Either way, it captures Elihu's youthful hesitation before launching into his lengthy speech.

senses.1: Spanish 'me-encogí' (I shrank back), English 'I-held-back'—both emphasizing the restraint born of fear. Job 32:6 introduces Elihu's speech, explaining why he waited: respect for age dictated silence, but now, frustrated by the friends' failure to answer Job, he must speak. The verb conveys both appropriate deference and the inner tension of someone bursting to contribute but constrained by social protocol.

gloss_terse: Zoheleth, 'the Stone of Zoheleth' near En-rogel (1 Kings 1:9); possibly meaning 'serpent' or 'sliding stone'
gloss_readable: Zoheleth appears as the name of a stone landmark near En-rogel where Adonijah held his abortive coronation feast. The name might mean 'serpent' or 'sliding/crawling thing,' though some scholars propose astronomical connections (the planet Saturn in Arabic). Others see it as a proper noun whose original meaning was lost even in antiquity. Whatever its etymology, the Stone of Zoheleth marks the site of Adonijah's failed bid for David's throne, a geographical anchor for a pivotal political moment.

senses.1: All translations simply transliterate: Spanish 'Zojelet,' English 'Zoheleth,' French and German matching. First Kings 1:9 locates Adonijah's feast precisely, and the Stone of Zoheleth functions as a known landmark. The name's obscurity to modern readers likely mirrors ancient uncertainty about its meaning. It stands as a mute witness to the dynastic struggles of David's old age, the place where Adonijah's ambitions culminated before Solomon's anointing undercut them.
